replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a wild fact to kick us off:

The word "bank" is a single token — but an LLM has no idea whether you mean a riverbank or a financial institution until it looks at the surrounding words.

That's not a quirk. It's the whole game.

---

**Tokenization** is the very first thing that happens when you hit send.

Your prompt doesn't enter the model as words — it gets sliced into chunks called tokens, which are then converted to numbers.

[EX]GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens. "Unbelievable" might be one token. "Tokenization" might be split into "Token" + "ization" — two tokens. A single emoji can be 3–4 tokens.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into a sequence of numbers — that's the only format a neural network can actually process.[/KEY]

Those numbers aren't random. Each token ID maps to a position in a giant table, and from there the model looks up a dense list of numbers called an **embedding** — a kind of coordinate in meaning-space where similar words land near each other.

That's the first step: text → tokens → numbers → embeddings.

---

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually convert your words into?
A) A dictionary lookup of definitions
B) A sequence of numbers the model can process
C) A compressed copy of your original sentence
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A sequence of numbers the model can process
replies.raw:
Exactly right — and notice what that rules out: the model never "reads" your words the way you do. It only ever sees numbers.

---

Now that the prompt is a sequence of number-vectors, the model needs to figure out which tokens *matter most* to each other.

That's where the **attention mechanism** comes in.

For every token in your prompt, attention asks: *which other tokens should I weight heavily when predicting what comes next?*

[EX]In the sentence "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired" — what does "it" refer to? The animal, not the street. Attention learns to connect "it" back to "animal" by assigning that pair a high weight.[/EX]

[KEY]Attention lets the model weigh relationships between tokens across the whole prompt — so distant words can still influence each other.[/KEY]

This happens in parallel across dozens of "attention heads," each one learning to track a different kind of relationship — grammar, coreference, topic, tone.

After attention does its work, the model has a rich, context-aware representation of your entire prompt.

---

[Q]
What problem does the attention mechanism solve?
A) It compresses long prompts so they fit in memory
B) It translates tokens back into readable words
C) It figures out which tokens should influence each other when building meaning
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) It compresses long prompts so they fit in memory
replies.raw:
Close — but that's actually a different problem that researchers work on separately (context windows and memory are real constraints, just not what attention is for).

Attention isn't about shrinking anything. It's about *relationships*.

Think of it this way: after tokenization, the model has a row of number-vectors but no sense of how they connect. Attention is what lets the model notice that "it" in your sentence points back to "animal" — not because it's close by, but because the relationship is meaningful.

Compression would throw information away. Attention does the opposite — it pulls relevant information *forward* into each token's representation.

---

Now you've got the full pipeline in place. Time for the last piece.

After attention builds a rich, context-aware representation of your prompt, the model does one thing: it predicts the single most likely **next token**.

Then it appends that token and repeats — predict, append, predict, append — until the response is done.

[EX]Give a model the prompt "The cat sat on the ___" and next-token prediction will assign high probability to "mat," "floor," "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." The model learned those weights from billions of sentences during training.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates text one token at a time, always predicting what comes next based on everything before it — never planning the whole response in advance.[/KEY]

---

[Q]
How does an LLM produce a full response?
A) It retrieves a pre-written answer from a database
B) It generates the entire response at once, then sends it
C) It predicts one token at a time, each building on the last
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) It predicts one token at a time, each building on the last
replies.raw:
You nailed it — and that one fact explains a lot. It's why AI can start a sentence confidently and then veer off in a weird direction halfway through. There's no outline, no plan — just the next most likely token, over and over.

A tokenizer chops your text into chunks called *tokens*. Sometimes a token is a whole word. Sometimes it's just a fragment.

The word "unhappiness" might become three tokens: "un", "happi", "ness". GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 possible tokens.

[EX]Try this: the sentence "I went to the bank" contains a hidden ambiguity — river bank or money bank? To the tokenizer, that doesn't matter yet. It just maps each word to a number ID and passes those IDs downstream. "bank" might become token #4912. That's it.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into a sequence of number IDs — the raw material every LLM starts with.[/KEY]

Before we go further, let's make sure this first piece is solid.

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually output when it processes your prompt?
A) A dictionary definition of each word
B) A sequence of number IDs representing text chunks
C) A search query sent to the internet
ANS: B
[/Q]
